**Chapter 1 · Section 3 of 4** · [The Chemical Core](index.qmd)

## Same leaves, different cup

You make a cup of tea, get distracted, and return to a brew that tastes quite different from yesterday's. The packet has not changed. The kettle has not changed. But the leaves have spent longer in the water.

That ordinary kitchen moment contains this lesson's question: **what are you changing when you change the way you brew?**

In the [previous lesson](02-processing.qmd), processing shaped the leaf before it reached you. Now water takes over. Brewing is **extraction**: compounds move from the leaf into the water. Time and temperature influence that process, and different compounds do not respond in identical ways.[^brewing]

You can explore the result with two cups, a timer, and tea you already own.

## Try it: two cups, one change {#try-it-two-cups-one-change}

For this comparison, use a tea whose packet gives a steeping time of a few minutes. You will make one cup at that time and another **two minutes longer**. These are comparison settings, not a claim about the best recipe for every tea.

1. **Set up a fair pair.** Use two similar mugs, equal portions of the same tea, and the same measured amount of water. Two matching tea bags are convenient; with loose leaves, weigh equal portions and use two similar infusers.
2. **Keep the water alike.** Use the packet's suggested temperature and pour from the same kettle in quick succession. Keep stirring, covering, and other handling the same.
3. **Change only the steeping time.** Start a timer for each pour. Remove the first bag or infuser at the suggested time and the second two minutes later. Do not squeeze either bag.
4. **Compare when comfortable to sip.** Smell each cup, then take small sips. Try to compare at similar drinking temperatures: a hotter sample can make the comparison harder. Leave milk and sugar out for this first tasting.

Use a few words, not a professional tasting vocabulary:

| Notice | Cup A: packet time | Cup B: two minutes longer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aroma: what does it remind you of? | | |
| Bitterness: mild, moderate, or strong? | | |
| Drying feeling after a sip: slight or pronounced? | | |
| Which would you choose to drink again, and why? | | |

**Bitterness is a taste; astringency is the drying or puckering sensation.** Try recording them separately. You might prefer the longer steep, prefer the shorter one, or find little difference. All three are useful observations.

This is a kitchen comparison, not a blinded laboratory test. Pouring, cooling, and knowing which cup is which can affect the result. Repeat it another day before treating your first impression as a rule.

## What happened while you waited?

Water wets the leaves, soluble material dissolves, and compounds move into the surrounding liquid. Brewing changes a mixture: aroma, color, taste, and mouthfeel give you different clues about that mixture. A darker cup is not a chemical assay.

Three familiar controls help you explore it:

| Control | What you change | How to use it in your next comparison |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Time** | How long water and leaves stay in contact | Keep the tea, water, and temperature fixed; compare two steeping times. |
| **Temperature** | The conditions under which extraction takes place | Keep the leaf amount and time fixed; compare two starting temperatures. |
| **Leaf-to-water ratio** | How much leaf is available for a given amount of water | Keep the water volume fixed; compare two weighed portions of leaf. |

Longer or hotter is not automatically better. Your preferred cup is a taste decision, not a contest to extract the largest possible amount.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: three compounds, without a fixed exit order"}
**Caffeine**, **L-theanine**, and **catechins** such as EGCG are useful names to recognize. But a simple story in which one always comes out first and another always comes out last is too tidy for real tea.

Keenan and colleagues found brewing time to be an important determinant of the amount of L-theanine in the cup; their measurements also differed between the teas tested.[^theanine] Saklar and colleagues measured changes in caffeine and individual catechins across brewing conditions.[^brewing] These results describe particular teas and methods, not a universal extraction timetable.

Also distinguish **solubility**—how much of a substance can dissolve under specified conditions—from **extraction from a leaf**. The latter involves the leaf material as well as the water. A solubility figure for an isolated compound is not a recipe for calculating its dose in your mug.
:::

## A research result worth reading carefully

Here is a concrete example of how to use a brewing paper without turning it into a commandment.

Saklar and colleagues brewed Turkish green tea at **75, 85, and 95°C**, using times from **1 to 45 minutes**. They measured compounds and asked **nine trained panelists** to assess the infusions. In that experiment, **85°C for 3 minutes** gave the highest EGCG content and the highest sensory scores.[^brewing]

That is an interesting result. It is also bounded by the tea, preparation method, and panel that produced it. It does **not** establish a perfect temperature for every green tea, a preferred recipe for every drinker, or a benefit to attention or health.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: why catechin measurements can stop rising"}
Extraction is not the only process taking place. In the same experiment, some catechin forms decreased with prolonged brewing while other forms increased. Heat can promote changes between related chemical forms, and degradation can also matter.[^brewing]

So “leave it longer to get more EGCG” is not an unlimited rule. The useful question is always: more of which compound, from which tea, under which conditions?
:::

## Two tempting shortcuts

### “It tastes gentle, so it must contain little caffeine.”

Your tasting notes describe the sensory experience. They do not measure caffeine. A smooth cup can still contain it, and comparing bitterness alone cannot give you a reliable caffeine dose. For quantities, consult the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd), keeping its brewing assumptions in view.

### “Cold water makes tea caffeine-free.”

Cold brewing still extracts caffeine. Research comparing hot, cold, and hot-then-iced preparations found that the outcome depended on tea type and preparation.[^cold] “Cold” describes the method; it is not a decaffeination claim. A cold brew and a hot brew also commonly differ in duration, so temperature alone does not explain the comparison.

## Give the leaves a second act

If you usually brew whole leaves, try another infusion as a separate exploration. Drain the first brew, add a measured amount of fresh water, and note the new time and temperature. Compare aroma, taste, and mouthfeel again.

Remember that this is a different question from the two-cup experiment: the leaves have already been wetted and extracted. You are exploring a sequence, not comparing two fresh portions under matched conditions. Let the notes describe what you actually notice; a softer taste alone does not establish that the second cup is caffeine-free.

## What to do with your result

Suppose your notes read: **“Cup A smells pleasant but tastes thin. Cup B has more body, but the finish is too drying.”** That is an illustrative result, not a prediction. A sensible next trial would keep everything else the same and try a time between the two. If both cups disappoint you, choose another control to investigate rather than changing the whole recipe at once.

The [Kitchen troubleshoot](../../tea-troubleshoot.qmd) guide gives more starting points. Keep the recipe beside the verdict: “two minutes, this much leaf, this much water” is something you can repeat. “Nice tea” is harder to reproduce.

::: {.callout-tip title="Take this to your next cup"}
Change one thing, write down what you notice, and keep taste separate from chemical measurement. You are learning how to make a cup you enjoy—and how to ask a better question about it.
:::

The next lesson introduces the [compounds behind the cup](04-compounds.qmd). For claims about what happens after drinking, [Reading a tea study](../../tea-reading-studies.qmd) helps you distinguish a brewing measurement from evidence about people.
